commonErrors.example: A learner writes on the worksheet that curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one.

fixIt.corrected: Curly arrows follow the electrons: they start at an electron-rich region (a lone pair or pi bond) and point to where the electrons go.
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: state what a curly arrow actually tracks, and where every arrow starts.

commonErrors.misconception: Curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one.

commonErrors.example: On the exit ticket, a learner picks the statement that curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one.

fixIt.corrected: The arrow starts at an electron-rich region, such as a lone pair or a pi bond, and points to where the electron pair goes
fixIt.prompt: Fix it: explain in one sentence why the pi bond, not an electron-poor atom, is where the first arrow of the ethene and HBr mechanism starts.

commonErrors.misconception: Curly arrows point from the electron-poor atom toward the electron-rich one.

modelAnswers.answer: The mechanism is SN1. The slow first step is the C-Br bond breaking on its own to form a planar carbocation and Br-, and hydroxide plays no part in that step, so the rate depends only on the halogenoalkane: rate = k[(CH3)3CBr]. Hydroxide attacks the carbocation in a second, fast step.
modelAnswers.question: A tertiary halogenoalkane, (CH3)3CBr, reacts with aqueous hydroxide. The rate is unchanged when the hydroxide concentration is doubled. Name the mechanism and explain the rate evidence.

modelAnswers.answer: Hydroxide attacks opposite the C-Br bond so its lone pair can form the new C-O bond as the C-Br pair leaves with bromine, through a single transition state. The rate equation, rate = k[CH3Br][OH-], includes both reactants, which shows both meet in the one slow step.
modelAnswers.question: In the SN2 reaction of CH3Br with OH-, why must the hydroxide attack from the back, and what does the rate equation tell you about the step?

nextSteps: Reteach the arrow trap from the paired notes trap before any further mechanism work: a curly arrow tracks one electron pair, and atoms stay put.
Practise explaining SN1 and SN2 from their rate equations, and check each arrow against the pi bond in scene s3 and the carbocation in scene s4.
strengths: Most of the class can name the SN1 mechanism from the rate evidence on the worksheet: the nucleophile is absent from the slow step, so the rate depends only on the halogenoalkane.
The class can explain the SN2 backside attack on the exit ticket: hydroxide attacks opposite the C-Br bond through a single transition state, and both reactants appear in the rate equation.
